articles.title: DHS touts highest ICE deportations in history, as Mullin says agency has been ‘unleashed’
articles.summary: DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin announced record ICE arrests and deportations in fiscal 2026, with arrests exceeding three Biden fiscal years combined.
articles.body: Immigration officials on Thursday announced a historic milestone, saying arrests and deportations this year reached the highest levels in the agency’s history, with arrests surpassing the combined totals of the Biden administration’s final three years and deportations nearly matching them. "Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history," Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Department of Homeland Security (DHS), said. "The total number of ICE arrests in Fiscal Year 2026 was more than all three full fiscal years under Biden combined, as the patriots of ICE work around the clock to make America safe again. Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, ICE has been unleashed to target and remove illegal aliens so that we can save American lives." Officials made more than 491,000 arrests, including nearly 475,000 administrative arrests, the highest administrative total in agency history. MULLIN VOWS ‘ZERO CHANGE’ ON IMMIGRATION AFTER REPUBLICANS SUFFER CRUSHING MIDTERM LOSSES ICE also carried out 483,200 deportations this fiscal year, surpassing the previous agency record of 442,640 set the year before. Total arrests exceeded the combined figures for fiscal years 2022, 2023 and 2024 under the Biden administration by nearly 65,000, DHS said. Meanwhile, deportations this fiscal year nearly matched the combined total for all three full fiscal years under Biden, falling short by fewer than 3,000, according to the department. WHITE HOUSE DOUBLES DOWN AFTER TRUMP ANGERS BASE BY FLOATING ILLEGAL ALIEN DEAL WITH DEMS Specifically, this year's arrests were more than six times higher than those recorded during former President Joe Biden's first fiscal year in office. Deportations were also more than eight times higher for the same time period. August 2026 also set a new record for arrests, with 50,925, marking the highest number for any single month in ICE history, Mullin said. That pace continued into September, which logged over 48,000 arrests, representing a more than 300% increase over the average September under the previous administration. articles.title: Iran says it targeted US radar site in Bahrain
articles.summary: IRGC says it hit radar in retaliation for an ‘enemy’ air attack on a telecom tower in Iran’s Hormozgan province.
articles.body:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has targeted a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for what it described as an air attack on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran.

The claim came hours after Iran’s state news agency IRNA, citing official sources, reported that the port city of Sirik in Hormozgan province was hit by “enemy fire” on Thursday.

In a statement carried by the semi-official Tasnim news agency, the IRGC called the strike a “serious warning” to the “aggressor enemy” to stop what it said was a series of aerial provocations and oil smuggling in the Strait of Hormuz.

“Should these violations and acts of aggression recur, the IRGC Aerospace Force stands in full readiness to engage without limits,” the statement said.

The IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency said the IRGC’s Aerospace Force had “targeted and destroyed” the radar installation.

There was no immediate comment from Washington or Manama.

Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet.

The Fifth Fleet headquarters, at the Naval Support Activity base in the capital, Manama, is the main command centre for US naval operations in the Middle East.

It was hit in the opening hours of the war on February 28, and satellite images analysed by Al Jazeera showed direct hits on several radar domes and damage to buildings across the base.

The US has reportedly reduced its troop numbers at bases in the region and ordered some diplomatic staff to leave, according to news outlets, as Trump weighs new strikes on Iran

US Central Command said it “regularly” moves personnel and assets to “optimise mission readiness”.

According to the Reuters news agency, it is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military assets in a Gulf country.

The claim comes as Israel’s security cabinet has ordered the military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran , according to Israeli media, including the public broadcaster KAN.

Iran’s security chief Mohsen Rezaei has warned that if the US launches another war, every military base involved, anywhere from West Asia to Europe, would be a legitimate target for Iranian strikes.

A Pentagon inspector general’s report released in September found that Iranian attacks damaged or destroyed hundreds of buildings at US installations in eight countries, including Bahrain, in the first four months of the war.

Analysts say several US bases in the region have been almost rendered unusable.

US President Donald Trump has said he is prepared to return to war if the diplomatic track offered by Qatar fails to deliver a deal.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has said economic pressure on Iran is working well enough that resuming large-scale military operations is unnecessary.

In an exclusive interview with Al Jazeera on Wednesday, Iran’s parliament speaker and lead negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the Strait of Hormuz would never go back to how it was before the war, and that “the ball is now in the American court “.

Meanwhile, US Central Command says its forces are still strictly enforcing the naval blockade on Iranian ports.

The war began on February 28 with US and Israeli attacks on Iran.

articles.title: 'How does a building just fall?' Neighbours grieve after deadly Brooklyn building collapse
articles.summary: The accident rattled the usually calm immigrant neighbourhood of Flatbush, New York. At least eight residents, including two children, died in the rubble.
articles.body:
What we know about the New York City building collapse

Over the loud noise of her radio, Ann Marie did not hear the sound of the Brooklyn building behind her home collapse on Wednesday night, but she soon saw the flashing lights of fire department trucks rushing to the scene.

When she made her way out to the wreckage, workers were still searching for bodies. One of the building's walls had torn off, exposing the inside of several apartment homes, and the rubble had collapsed into a construction site next door.

At least eight of her neighbours died in the accident - six adults and two children, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. Five of the victims were residents, CBS reported.

"Right now, I'm really scared," Marie told the BBC. "Now that I'm seeing exactly this side of the building, you can imagine the fright of those people, what happened to them."

On Thursday afternoon, Mamdani said he had visited survivors in hospital. Eighteen people were injured, including four firefighters. One person is in critical condition.

"I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost," Mamdani added. "These were our friends and our neighbours, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Trinidad and beyond."

Later on Thursday, a senior official with the New York Police Department identified the victims as Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9, Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31, Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10, Barry Mamadou, 23, and Ndiaye Mamadou, 31, according to CBS. They were residents of the building that collapsed.

The other three victims lived elsewhere. Gabriel Siguencia, 22, lived in the Bronx, Edgar Sapon, 26, lived in Hell's Kitchen and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26, lived in the Bushwick neighbourhood of Brooklyn.

It was around 16:00 EST (21:00 GMT) on Wednesday when residents heard a loud boom as the 1930s building collapsed into a neighbouring construction site, where crews were working, according to fire department officials. Two construction workers were among the dead.

The New York City Fire Department was on the scene within one minute of the emergency call, Mamdani said.

Patricia Starek was waiting for her son to come home from school last night when she saw the helicopters near her home. The surge of the emergency responders initially brought back memories of New York during 2001 terrorist attacks. She has lived in Flatbush for 26 years, including during 9/11.

"How does a building just fall into a pit? We all live here with the assumption that stairs are stable, floors are stable, that you can be on your third floor and not have the earth fall below you," she said.

Mamdani said search conditions would grow more difficult with the rain in the morning, and responders continued their efforts for about 24 hours before determining on Thursday afternoon that there were no more victims at the site. Workers looked through the wreckage with drones, sniffer dogs, cranes and other equipment.

Officials had said they would continue to search the wreckage until they were entirely certain there was no one left trapped, saying they still had big pieces of debris to remove.

The mayor said city officials had identified the companies running the construction site, and were examining 100 other sites operated by the same groups to ensure they are safe.

Contains some scenes which some viewers may find upsetting. - Video shows survivor being pulled from collapsed building in New York

Dozens of residents gathered around the building on Thursday morning as debris floated through the air, and they watched in horror as workers tried to find more survivors or recover remains.

The incident has rattled their calm and quiet neighbourhood, a melting pot of many New York immigrant communities including Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic and Asian residents.

Joyette Kerr had been at the scene since midnight, praying with family members who were missing loved ones.

At 1:30 EST (6:30 GMT), Kerr watched emergency responders pull a survivor from the wreckage.

At the church across the street, she consoled the wife of a young construction worker who died when the building fell on him. Rescuers recovered his body, Kerr said.

"His wife was very hysterical," said Kerr, who has lived in the neighbourhood since she was a teenager. "She couldn't take the pain."

She said another man had been frantically going to all the nearby hospitals to try to find his two nephews, but still had no answers.

Footage showed another woman who was six-months pregnant being rescued from the rubble.

"She is alive. She is still alive. I'm very happy. I'm very happy," her husband told the BBC's US partner CBS News. "I thank all of you guys."

Starek, the longtime Flatbush resident, said she was heading to the local YMCA where some family members were gathered to see if she could help - and many others in the neighbourhood were doing the same.

"People look out for each other," Marie said. To lose eight of her neighbours, she said: "I can't believe it. There's a pain."

Kerr said she hoped her hours with the victims' families brought them some measure of comfort after one of the deadliest building collapses in recent New York history.

"It's going to be very profound," she said of the impact the accident will have. "Hopefully this will bring the community together."

articles.title: Stephen A Smith debriefs interview with President Trump, warns Democrats face steep challenge
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith says President Trump was "immovable" in refusing to accept blame for GOP midterm losses during their wide-ranging White House interview.
articles.body: ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith debriefed his White House interview with President Donald Trump during an appearance Thursday on "Hannity" and cautioned Democrats over the influence of the party's far-left flank. Smith said the pair discussed "devastating" GOP midterm losses during a 40-minute, wide-ranging interview and criticized Trump for refusing to take blame, saying he was "immovable" on that point. "We talked about the devastating losses in the midterms and how the GOP essentially got slaughtered," Smith told Fox News host Sean Hannity. "I asked him, is he willing to point the finger at himself, and he was dogged… he was immovable in that regard," he added. DOUG SCHOEN: THE BIGGEST WINNER AND THE BIGGEST LOSER IN THE 2026 MIDTERMS Trump repeatedly told Americans during his midterm blitz to vote as if he were on the ballot, but Smith said the commander-in-chief removed himself from that narrative during their Thursday interview. "He said, ‘I wasn't on the ballot.’ I said, ‘That makes absolutely no sense, Mr. President. You said, put you on a ballot. articles.title: Iranophobia: Netanyahu’s bid to transform fear into political survival
articles.summary: Despite knowing a war with Iran would be manufactured for Netanyahu’s survival, many would still rally behind it.
articles.body:
As the right-wing coalition government that oversaw the genocide in Gaza, launched attacks across the region, and eroded civil liberties at home appears to lose its grip on power by the day, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s increasingly frantic efforts to derail the political transition suggest a growing desperation to stay in office.

Among those efforts appears to be an attempt to reignite the war with Iran. Netanyahu has reportedly ordered the Israeli military to prepare for war ahead of a potential attack on Iran, in defiance of the opposition’s calls for restraint.

The reports follow revelations that Netanyahu had been phoning US President Donald Trump almost daily to press for renewed strikes on Iran. Israeli media have also reported repeated confrontations between Netanyahu and military chief Eyal Zamir, who has resisted proposals for military action against Iran, warning that they could trigger a wider conflict.

Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot has been tasked with forming a viable government, but that is not a foregone conclusion. Netanyahu has been pushing for a national unity government that would include himself and his Likud party, or waiting for Eisenkot to fail, leading to another election.

“Netanyahu is desperate,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli political analyst at King’s College London, said. “He knows – and you can see it from his behaviour – that it is likely that he is politically done, and only a national unity government could save him.”

“A little war could compel Eisenkot & Co,” he said, referring to the opposition bloc and its leader, Gadi Eisenkot, “to form such a government in a time of crisis.”

Many in the opposition, including Eisenkot himself, have accused Netanyahu of attempting to drag the country into a potentially devastating war for his own political survival, or of deliberately stalling the coalition-building process in the hope of running down the clock and forcing another election.

Yet while critics see Netanyahu’s attempts to reignite war with Iran as a cynical bid to retain power, analysts have suggested that even his fiercest opponents could rally behind him if he does launch an attack.

“It’s paradoxical,” said Haggai Ram, a professor at Ben-Gurion University and author of the book Iranophobia, which details Israel’s longstanding hostility to Tehran. “Everyone knows it would be contrived, but the hysteria over Iran cuts through everything. If Netanyahu succeeds, and manages to start a war with Iran, of course the opposition would fall in behind him, and the public would expect them to. They’d recognise the cynicism for what it was, but this is Iran. This is the great enemy.”

“For the former military members of the opposition, confronting Iran was what they spent their entire lives training for. For the public, after years of being told of the Iranian threat, many already see the war as inevitable,” he said.

Israel’s decades-long cold war with Iran has been a constant throughout much of the Israeli population’s lifetime. For decades, Israelis have lived with the threat of attacks from Iran’s regional allies, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, whose rhetoric threatening Israel’s destruction has been widely reported in Israeli media.

That fear has been reinforced by repeated warnings from Israeli leaders, dating back to at least the 1990s, that Tehran was on the brink of acquiring a nuclear weapon and would likely use it against Israel.

Tensions came to a head as Israel launched multiple wars across the region following the Hamas-led attack on October 7, 2023. A 12-day exchange of strikes with Iran in June 2025 was followed by a joint attack with the US launched in February, which has disrupted some of the world’s critical waterways, thrown financial markets into turmoil, and affected household expenditure across much of the world.

Nevertheless, another war with Iran may offer Netanyahu a route out of the political bind he finds himself in, political psychologist Daniel Bar-Tal of Tel Aviv University suggested.

As things stand, a majority of the public oppose him and his coalition, and, in Bar-Tal’s framing, he is “fighting for his life”, with multiple active criminal cases against him.

Although Bar-Tal doubted that Trump, Israel’s principal ally and military backer, would allow Netanyahu to derail US negotiations with Iran, he believed that Israelis would still “support such a war, and this is a good card for him to play [to create the] turmoil” needed to extricate himself from his current predicament.

For now, Ram said, Israel maintains what, for many, feels like a state of permanent expectation.

“People know that any case for war would be manufactured,” he said. “They’re not stupid and they see it for what it is. However, many people – including some of my friends and students – regard it as inevitable. They’re just waiting, and if and when it happens, despite everything they know, they will still report for duty and do what they’re ordered.”

articles.title: UNRWA funding cuts deepen hardship for Palestinian refugees in Lebanon
articles.summary: Funding cuts and Israel’s war have left Palestinians in Lebanon in increasingly dire circumstances.
articles.body:
Beirut, Lebanon – Doumoua al-Baitan sat on the roof of a building in Beirut’s Palestinian refugee camp of Bourj el-Barajneh as the sun set. Like many Palestinian refugees in Lebanon, al-Baitan was born and raised in this camp.

For decades, Palestinians in Lebanon have been supported by the UN branch focused on Palestinian refugees, UNRWA. But funding cuts have impeded UNRWA’s ability to provide crucial aid, particularly since the Trump administration’s decision in February 2025 to maintain a US funding freeze imposed the previous year.

Between the funding cuts and funding shortfalls, UNRWA has had to close down or reduce hours of schools, healthcare centres, and clinics in Lebanon’s Palestinian refugee camps.

Palestinians told Al Jazeera that in addition to there being less work to go around and less medical support, children are being crammed into overcrowded classrooms, and the use and sale of illegal drugs has become more prevalent.

“My kids cannot retain what they are taught in class,” al-Baitan said, citing overcrowding. The divorced mother of four said she has started paying $200 per month – the same price as her monthly rent – for two of her children to attend after-school lessons.

Since 1950, UNRWA has supported Palestinian refugees across the Middle East. Lebanon has 12 Palestinian refugee camps, where a large proportion of the country’s approximately 230,000 Palestinians live.

UNRWA’s role in the camps includes providing education, healthcare, relief and social services, camp infrastructure and improvement, microfinance, and emergency assistance. Palestinians first became refugees in Lebanon during the 1948 Nakba, when Zionist forces established the state of Israel after turning 750,000 Palestinians into refugees.

Today, the majority of Palestinians in Lebanon are de facto stateless and do not have Lebanese citizenship. As a result, they are effectively banned from a number of professions in Lebanon, including medicine, law, engineering, and pharmacy, which has meant the community is one of the most vulnerable in Lebanon. And that vulnerability has only increased as UNRWA faces a severe funding shortfall.

UNRWA spokesperson Fadi al-Tayyar told Al Jazeera in October that his agency needed around $70m to $80m more for 2026, forcing them to reduce service working hours by 20 percent since February.

Many schools have been forced to reduce the school week from five to four days for the 2026-27 academic year. More than 35,000 pupils are in 58 schools, with 15 additional classrooms in the northern Beddawi camp, in Tripoli.

Residents in Bourj el-Barajneh said that most of the schools in the camp had been shut down and that now students were being crammed into classrooms of 40 or more students at a time.

According to a monthly report released by the Jafra Foundation, a nonprofit that supports vulnerable communities in Lebanon including Palestinian refugees, the funding shortfall “threatens the education, healthcare, water, and sanitation services provided by UNRWA and exacerbates the pressures on millions of Palestinian refugees in its five areas of operation: the Gaza Strip, the West Bank (including East Jerusalem), Jordan, Lebanon, and Syria”.

UNRWA’s June 2026 emergency report found that out of 26 primary healthcare centres and clinics, only 15 were operational. Eleven had shut down.

While the precarity has had an impact on the Palestinian community in Lebanon at large, some refugees also suffer from compounding difficulties. There are between 3,000 and 5,000 Palestinian refugees who are undocumented.

There are also an estimated 19,000 Palestinian refugees from Syria living in Lebanon, many of whom fled Lebanon’s eastern neighbour during the country’s 13-year war. A policy change in Lebanon in May 2024, however, halted residency renewals for many Palestinians from Syria, leading to increased exposure to detention, more difficulty in finding legal employment, and registering for education or civil issues.

Locals and experts also said the funding shortcomings have led to a proliferation of issues related to drugs and violence in the camps.

“There is a very tired economic situation and there is no work,” Fadi Abu Halawa, the security officer at the Jafra Foundation in Beirut, told Al Jazeera. He added that Jafra’s monthly report showed an increase in crime and drug use and distribution in the camps.

“Of course, all of this is 100 percent due to the economy,” he said.

People in the camps have responded to the funding cuts, lack of work, and subpar services by organising sit-ins. Shatila camp, one of the largest in Beirut, has organised one for Friday.

“The recent distribution of bread and flour by UNRWA has sparked widespread dissatisfaction among Palestinian refugees in the camps,” Jafra’s October report says. “They considered that allocating a 5-kilogram bag of flour to each family does not meet the needs of households, especially large ones, and does not compensate for the reduction in services and aid on which they depend.”

Israel’s war on Lebanon has also had an impact on the camps. Five of Lebanon’s camps are located in southern Lebanon and have faced displacement and attacks. Israel killed 12 people in attacks across Lebanon in February, including two in Ein el-Hilweh, Lebanon’s biggest Palestinian camp, located in the southern city of Sidon. Three months before that, it had killed at least 13 people, including 11 children, who were playing football in the dense camp.

The Jafra report from October says the camps “have been witnessing a state of security instability with the recent Israeli escalation in military operations in southern Lebanon, amid fears that these operations are approaching the camps, which may lead to a new wave of displacement of refugee families”.

articles.title: Burkina Faso’s rival armed groups turn on each other as state loses ground
articles.summary: JNIM and ISIL intensify their fight for control as Burkina Faso struggles to contain the wider armed conflict.
articles.body:
Ouagadougou, Burkina Faso – Armed fighters from two rival groups have fought a series of increasingly deadly battles along Burkina Faso’s northern border with Mali, as the government struggles to reassert control over large parts of the country.

The clashes between Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM), an al-Qaeda affiliate, and the ISIL affiliate in Sahel Province (ISSP) have intensified since early September, with both groups competing for territory and influence across the borderlands. Their latest confrontations have produced competing claims of heavy casualties, although the figures released by the ISIL (ISIS) group remain unverified.

One of the first major confrontations took place near Kacham, close to the Mali border, in early September. ISSP claimed to have killed more than 200 JNIM fighters, captured more than 30 others and seized weapons and motorcycles. The claim has not been independently verified. Heni Nsaibia, of the monitoring group Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), said that, if confirmed, the reported death toll would make it the deadliest battle recorded between the two groups.

The fighting escalated again on October 9 around Ganadaouri, in Burkina Faso’s northern Oudalan province. ISIL’s weekly publication, Al-Naba, subsequently claimed that more than 400 JNIM fighters had been killed. JNIM has not publicly responded to the claim, and no independent assessment has established the number of casualties.

The scale of the claim came under further scrutiny when ISSP published photographs on November 1 presented as evidence of its victory, showing what it described as the aftermath of the battle.

Regional news outlet i-Sahel counted at least 120 bodies in the images but said it could not independently verify whether those pictured were victims of the reported fighting. The number visible in the photos is considerably below the 400 deaths claimed by ISIL.

A rivalry that is becoming increasingly costly

The confrontation is part of a rivalry that has persisted since 2019, when the two groups began fighting over territory, influence and access to local populations across the Sahel. Their competition has become increasingly costly, with ACLED recording around 320 armed confrontations between them and more than 2,200 fighter deaths since the conflict began.

The fighting comes as JNIM continues to make gains against government forces in Burkina Faso. The International Crisis Group says the group holds extensive areas of the country, particularly in the north, north-central region, west and east. Its influence has allowed it to challenge state authority across several regions while maintaining operations in neighbouring Mali and Niger.

ACLED’s March 2026 overview documented more than 30 JNIM attacks in Burkina Faso during a February offensive against the military and state-backed Volunteers for the Defense of the Homeland (VDP).

The attacks resulted in the deaths of more than 120 soldiers, forest guards and militia fighters, according to the conflict monitor. The campaign illustrated the pressure facing government forces, even as JNIM had to contend with attacks from its Islamic State rival.

The rivalry could offer Burkina Faso’s authorities some breathing room if JNIM is forced to divert fighters and resources to defend its positions against ISSP.

But there is little reason to assume that the infighting will translate into lasting gains for the government. JNIM remains active across several countries, while ISSP’s battlefield successes could strengthen its position in areas where the two groups compete.

The government faces a wider security crisis

For communities caught between the armed groups and government forces, the prospect of one organisation weakening another offers little certainty of relief. Burkina Faso’s security crisis has displaced millions of people and disrupted access to farmland, markets and basic services.

The scale of the humanitarian crisis remains severe. An estimated 4.5 million people in Burkina Faso need humanitarian assistance in 2026, according to United Nations humanitarian planning figures. The last consolidated official estimate of internal displacement, published in March 2023, put the number at approximately 2.1 million. That figure should not be mistaken for a newly verified 2026 count.

A citizen of Niger, who spoke to Al Jazeera on condition of anonymity because of security concerns, said the fighting between the two groups had raised hopes that communities in the borderlands might face less pressure.

“In Tillaberi, where I have family members, our people have endured too much fear. If JNIM and ISSP keep fighting each other, the danger to our communities may lessen, since their forces may weaken. People here deserve the chance to work their fields, travel safely, and raise their children without fearing attacks from either group.”

The rivalry is no longer confined to Burkina Faso and Mali. ACLED has documented its spread into Niger’s Tillaberi and Dosso regions and Nigeria’s Kebbi State, adding to concerns that the conflict is reaching further into West Africa.

The conflict monitor recorded more than 10,000 deaths from political violence across Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger between January 1 and November 28, 2025.

JNIM’s expansion raises concern across West Africa

Viraj Pattni, a senior associate at Castor Vali, a security risk management company, told Al Jazeera that JNIM’s expanding operations in the region could increase the threat to countries along the Gulf of Guinea.

“The threat of Islamist militancy spreading to coastal countries is very real,” Pattni explained. “Over the past 24 months, JNIM in particular has expanded the intensity of their operations in western and southern Mali. The group has established at least one training camp in the Sikasso Region of Mali, meaning they are well-positioned to continue building their fighting capacity along the border with Ivory Coast.”

“Although the group’s activity isn’t as pronounced in southern regions of Burkina Faso, the epicentre of Islamist militancy in the region, their stranglehold over the Est Region enabled the group to expand and intensify their operations in Togo and Benin in 2025,” he said.

“The group’s activity extended noticeably further into Benin in 2025, and they also claimed their first official attack in Nigeria’s Kwara State in October 2025,” Pattni added.

“Over the longer term, several underlying factors contribute to their likely continued expansion into littoral West Africa, such as porous borders, high levels of marginalisation in northern regions of littoral West African countries and communal tensions, particularly anti-Fulani sentiment.”

ISSP puts pressure on JNIM’s regional dominance

For Nsaibia, of conflict monitor ACLED, the growing confrontation between the two groups could force JNIM to reconsider how it allocates its resources across the region. He said the group had struggled to counter ISSP, which had repeatedly emerged victorious from some of their most significant battles in recent years.

“These increasingly deadly confrontations are forcing JNIM to divert fighters and resources from its primary objective of fighting government forces and allied militias in Mali and Burkina Faso,” Nsaibia said.

articles.title: London aphasia group write song about their experiences
articles.summary: Tens of thousands of Londoners live with aphasia, which impacts speech, reading and writing.
articles.body:
A group of Londoners with a brain condition that impacts their ability to speak, read, write and understand others have written a song about their experiences.

The Aphasia New Music Group, which is made up of people living with aphasia, musicians, and speech and language therapists, co-create music to raise awareness of the condition and support each other.

Aphasia is often caused by a stroke or brain injury. Tens of thousands of Londoners live with aphasia, according to the Stroke Association, and it can be very isolating.

Finn Beans, lead facilitator in the group and artistic director, said the song Listen was created to help people understand what it meant to live with the condition.

Dr Carolyn Bruce, speech and language therapist at University College London, works with the group.

"It's an acquired language difficulty and it happens as a result of brain injury, and it can affect all sorts of language skills," she said.

"It can affect reading or writing, speaking, understanding, and as a result it makes life very challenging for people after their stroke, and it stops them engaging in the life they had before that happened."

Colin Lyall was one of the group's first members.

"I had a stroke 13 years ago and I had aphasia," he said. "In the hospital I could say sort of yes and no.

"My intelligence was intact but I couldn't get any words right.

"So I went back home and I had speech and language therapy... and my words are kind of getting better, and I think now I'm not 100% but I still want to be better."

Lyall said his speech had improved but his reading and writing skills were not as good as they used to be.

What happened to him led him to set up a charity called Say Aphasia that supports people living with the condition. He said the music group was also critical to his development.

It is hoped that the song will counter misconceptions about aphasia, encourage connection and provide those with the condition with an outlet of shared understanding.

Beans said: "There's not a lot of understanding around what [aphasia] is, let alone what it means to live with it.

"We thought it'd be a really good chance to raise awareness.

"We don't always write a song just about what it's like to live with aphasia. We also explore sort of abstract concepts or incidental experiences that people have had.

"But with this song, Listen, we felt it was really important actually to have a clear message and to use it as a tool to raise awareness of aphasia, because typically in the UK most people haven't heard of it."

articles.title: Jersey politicians back focus on cost of living
articles.summary: The Government of Jersey's key priorities are passed despite concerns over a lack of "real action".
articles.body:
Politicians have backed the Government of Jersey's key priorities for the next political term which includes action on the cost of living.

States members adopted the Common Strategic Policy which lays out the Council of Ministers' priorities for the political term until 2030.

The priorities are centered around four pillars including targeted action on the cost of living, restoring Jersey's competitiveness, investing in homes and infrastructure and maintaining financial stability.

Chief Minister Lyndon Farnham said the government was determined "to make Jersey a more affordable place to live" but Reform Jersey co-leader Lyndsay Feltham said the policy lacked "real action".

The policy was backed with 31 votes in favour, 10 against and two abstentions.

Ministers first published the proposed policy in September and this week politicians debated a number of amendments proposed by backbenchers.

This included adding a priority about government transparency and promoting democracy , bringing the total number of priorities up from 11 to 12.

Deputy Feltham's amendments to add actions to the policy about household affordability and employment rights were rejected and members also voted not to include reference to rental stress.

The Reform Jersey co-leader said she was worried about the gaps this left behind.

"What I really wanted to see from government was something more sustained and a sustained commitment to reduce everyday cost of living," said Feltham.

"They've committed to a review of household affordability. A review doesn't put food on the table or a roof over somebody's head.

"I am really concerned that ministers aren't going to actually take any action."

However, the chief minister said the policy recognised islanders' concerns such as affordability, housing, economic growth, investing in infrastructure and protecting the environment.

In his closing speech, Farnham said their contributions "reflected a shared commitment to securing the best possible future for our island".

He said the policy "will send an important message to islanders that we are putting their interests before our political disagreements".

articles.title: In 2025, Alabama Power offered a landowner $80,000 for an easement across his property; in 2026, he won a ruling against its 300-foot exclusion request as the fight over his 416 acres continues
articles.summary: A dispute over a sprawling Alabama property has taken another turn after a judge rejected a utility company’s attempt to keep the landowner away from
articles.body: A dispute over a sprawling Alabama property has taken another turn after a judge rejected a utility company’s attempt to keep the landowner away from construction crews working on his land. Alabama Power has now taken the matter to the state’s highest court, prolonging a legal battle over a major electricity transmission project. According to reports by WVTM 13, 1819 News and Birmingham Free Press, the dispute centres on 416 acres owned by Fenn Church near Calera in Shelby County, where the company is seeking to build part of a 74-mile transmission line. The latest development came on November 10, when Shelby County Circuit Judge Jonathan Spann denied Alabama Power’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have required Church and visitors to remain at least 300 feet away from crews clearing trees on the property. The judge dismissed the case without prejudice, meaning the utility is not permanently barred from pursuing similar legal relief.Alabama Power subsequently filed a notice of appeal with the Alabama Supreme Court, seeking to challenge the decision. The company is also seeking transcripts and other court records as part of the appeal. The immediate disagreement centres on the company’s efforts to clear a construction corridor through Church’s land. Alabama Power maintains that the exclusion zone is necessary to protect the property owner, visitors and workers operating heavy machinery. Church, however, has opposed further clearing while his separate legal challenge to the easement remains unresolved.The disagreement has already resulted in several confrontations between Church and construction crews. According to earlier reporting by WVTM 13, workers had cleared hundreds of yards of the proposed corridor, including sections containing mature oak trees. Church has objected to the removal of vegetation and has repeatedly attempted to prevent crews from continuing their work.The wider dispute dates back to January 2025, when Alabama Power reportedly offered Church $80,000 for a permanent easement across his property. Subsequent offers increased to $132,000 in September 2025 and $194,000 in May 2026, according to court-related details reported by Birmingham Free Press.After negotiations failed, Alabama Power pursued eminent domain proceedings to secure the rights required for the project. On August 4, 2026, a probate court awarded Church $425,435 for the easement and access road rights. The compensation covers the utility’s right to use the designated portion of the property, not ownership of the entire land. Church challenged the award, and the separate condemnation case remains pending.The legal situation shifted again in September, when Judge Spann granted Church a preliminary injunction preventing Alabama Power from entering his property while the condemnation dispute continued. However, the Alabama Supreme Court stayed that injunction on October 21, allowing the utility to resume work. Crews returned to the property the following day.Alabama Power maintains that it has secured the necessary easement rights and that delays could jeopardise the project’s planned completion in May 2027. The Autaugaville-East Pelham 230-kilovolt transmission line is a 74-mile infrastructure project connecting the Montgomery and Birmingham areas. The company says it is needed to strengthen electricity supply for approximately three million customers across Alabama.Church has also raised the possibility of an alternative route through adjoining properties, arguing that the existing alignment would significantly affect his land and privacy. Alabama Power, however, has said that proposed alternatives were evaluated and considered unfeasible, citing additional costs, construction complications and potential delays. With the latest appeal, the dispute now has another legal chapter ahead. articles.title: US reports record number of deportations and arrests in 2026
articles.summary: ICE carried out 483,200 deportations in 2026. Democrats prepare to investigate tactics used.
articles.body:
The United States government has reported a historic high in deportations and arrests this fiscal year, surpassing previous records.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced on Wednesday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) carried out 483,200 deportations and more than 491,000 immigration arrests in 2026.

The total number of deportations breaks all records in ICE’s 23-year history, including the previous record of 442,640 deportations made in 2025.

The report comes days after US President Donald Trump acknowledged his administration’s immigration crackdown may have been “too tough”.

“Fiscal Year 2026 saw the highest number of ICE deportations and arrests for any year in ICE’s history. September 2026 was the best September in ICE’s history in terms of arrests,” Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

ICE said it made more than 48,000 arrests in September, ending a two-month run of record highs that reached 50,925 in August.

“There is no question the administration has increased enforcement more than any prior president. There’s also evidence that the illegal immigrant population has declined significantly because of increased out-migration due to a fear of enforcement,” Steven Camarota, director of research for the Washington, DC-based Center for Immigration Studies (CIS), told Al Jazeera.

However, he highlighted ambiguity in the figures DHS released.

“Of course the data is always incomplete and it’s difficult to measure. On the specific numbers released today, the big issue that I have not been able to determine is what percentage of these individuals are interior enforcement and what percentage are removals from the interior of the United States and what percentage are those turned around at the border or at airport.

“Increased removals, sometimes called deportation, certainly can encourage more people to go home, and clearly that is a central goal of this administration,” Camarota concluded.

Trump has acknowledged that his administration’s immigration policies “might be too tough”.

“A lot of people would say it is great but a lot of people would think it is too tough,” Trump said in a recent interview with CBS’s 60 Minutes.

Trump, however, defended his performance. “For getting people out, I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out; I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation or breaking of the law that was they came into the country illegally.”

Trump’s immigration crackdown has become a political vulnerability , with his approval rating on the issue falling to 38 percent from 50 percent at the start of his presidency, based on Reuters/Ipsos polling.

The Democrats appear to be gearing up to halt Trump’s immigration crackdown when they take control of Congress next year. They plan to target ICE tactics ⁠and expand paths to legal status, despite limits on ⁠how much they can achieve.

“We will investigate the administration weaponising DHS against Americans (and) its out of control immigration policies,” Bennie Thompson, a Mississippi Democrat and the soon-to-be chair of the House Homeland Security Committee, told the Reuters news agency in a statement.

At a news conference in the US Capitol with House members and newly elected representatives from southwestern border states, Henry Cuellar, a centrist Texas Democrat, ‌said he had already had conversations with Trump officials about focusing deportation efforts on criminals.

“We’re not going to be extreme,” Cuellar said, nodding to conservative voters across the US who cast their votes for Democrats.

But a number of Democratic voices sounded firmer.

“We will rip ICE apart,” Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan said while celebrating her triumph in Minnesota, where federal immigration agents shot dead two people during an enforcement surge in January.

Two US citizens, Alex Pretti and Renee Nicole Good, were killed in Minneapolis, in incidents that were caught on bystander video.

Their shooting deaths have gone viral, prompting international outrage. Other footage shows masked agents deploying chemical agents and beating civilians who were documenting their activities or protesting – activities protected under the US Constitution.

articles.title: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
articles.summary: Hall has been seeking a US visa in South Africa as other African beauty queens face similar hurdles.
articles.body:
Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.

Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.

"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.

Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.

"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.

Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.

In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.

Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.

The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.

Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.

"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.

Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."

In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.

She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"

The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

articles.title: The Gulf must build security that can outlast this war
articles.summary: Trump’s latest statement should accelerate the region’s move towards a layered and networked security architecture.
articles.body:
On November 10, Gulf defence ministers approved the establishment of a forward command in Kuwait under the Gulf Cooperation Council’s Unified Military Command, with forces to be allocated to it. The decision marks another step towards Gulf states taking greater collective responsibility for their security.

One day earlier, after meeting Qatar’s prime minister, US President Donald Trump had said: “Iran militarily is effectively over.” He also said the US blockade would continue and left open further military action. His remarks fell short of announcing an agreed end to the war.

Any opening for diplomacy deserves support. But even a lasting agreement would leave the Gulf’s underlying security problems unresolved. The Kuwait command’s value will depend on implementation and on how it connects with the region’s other security partnerships.

The answer requires abandoning the expectation that one grand security arrangement can resolve every threat facing the region. That expectation assumes a degree of agreement about enemies, priorities and acceptable risks that does not exist.

Iran’s attacks on Gulf states during this war, together with Israel’s September 2025 strike on Qatar, demonstrate the breadth of the challenge. A security architecture designed around only one adversary will leave serious gaps. Armed militias and terrorist groups add other risks, alongside cyberattacks, maritime disruption and the consequences of state failure in the neighbourhood. The erosion of international restraints on the use of force makes all of these problems harder to manage.

The most credible response to this complex set of threats is a security architecture that is both layered and networked. Gulf states are already moving in this direction. The task now is to make those arrangements work together and sustain the effort when the immediate pressure of war recedes.

Layering starts with the recognition that different partnerships do different jobs. National capabilities and cooperation within the Gulf Cooperation Council provide the foundation. The relationship with the United States remains central, while additional arrangements address needs that a single partner cannot meet.

Cooperation with US Central Command supplies an operational layer. The air and missile defence coordination cell opened at Al Udeid in January, for example, was designed to improve regional coordination, share threat warnings and prepare for contingencies.

The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed in August by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan, adds a collective defence commitment among its members. The Badr memorandum, signed in October by Qatar, Turkiye, Pakistan and Indonesia, sets out cooperation in defence manufacturing, research and technical training.

These arrangements should be judged by the gaps they fill. Collective defence, operational coordination and industrial capacity reinforce one another, but none can substitute for the others. Buying an interceptor, producing its components and deciding who will use it in a crisis are separate problems.

The next step is to connect these layers so that capabilities developed through one partnership strengthen what countries can do through another. This is what makes the architecture networked.

Qatar offers a useful example. It shares GCC membership with Saudi Arabia and participates in Badr alongside Turkiye and Pakistan. It therefore connects to all three Mecca signatories through other arrangements, despite not being a party to Mecca itself.

Those connections create opportunities. Stronger production capacity or better coordination among shared partners could improve the capabilities available to Qatar through its own relationships. A more effective deterrent against attacks on a neighbour could also improve the wider security environment.

Such benefits depend on deliberate cooperation. Qatar acquires no automatic Mecca guarantee through association. Information, equipment and expertise travel through a network only when governments agree to make that possible. The connections need as much attention as the agreements themselves.

This is also where the Gulf’s interests converge with those of a wider group of countries. European states, Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Indonesia and Pakistan all have reasons to resist a world in which force routinely overrides sovereignty and access to trade depends on political coercion.

Energy exporters and importers face different consequences when shipping is disrupted, but both need these routes to remain open. Countries need not share a political system or an identical relationship with Washington to recognise the costs of an international order becoming less predictable.

There is already a diplomatic basis for cooperation. The EU and GCC have jointly defended freedom of navigation through Hormuz. ASEAN and GCC ministers have reaffirmed sovereignty, the protection of civilian infrastructure and the need for diplomacy.

These states should become more active defenders of the basic rules on which their prosperity depends. They have an opportunity to shape the emerging international order collectively. Their combined economic, technological and diplomatic resources can give weight to rules that individual states struggle to defend alone. The same networks that help protect infrastructure can support coordinated diplomacy when those rules are violated.

Credibility will require consistency. Sovereignty must matter when the aggressor is a partner as well as an adversary. Civilian protection must apply in Palestine, Ukraine and the Gulf. Mediation must remain possible even when the parties at the table are politically inconvenient.

At the operational level, the immediate task is to connect existing security arrangements. Gulf governments and their partners should agree on how warnings can be shared across arrangements, which capabilities can be made available, and who has authority to request assistance. Joint exercises should test those connections under pressure, including when one partner cannot participate.

The next priority is protecting the systems that allow societies to function. Energy and water facilities, ports and communications networks deserve sustained cooperation on protection and repair. A partnership that can restore an essential service quickly contributes directly to security, even if it has no mutual defence clause.

Diplomacy to prevent escalation must form a layer of its own. Channels with Iran, arrangements to prevent incidents at sea and mechanisms for managing escalation remain necessary alongside stronger defences. Gulf states should use any opening created by the current talks to pursue reciprocal, verifiable restraint.

This wider security architecture would give Gulf, European and Asian partners practical work around which to organise. Some can contribute defence technology, others maritime expertise, industrial production, financing or diplomatic access. Cooperation should allow states to contribute where they have both the capacity and the political willingness to act.

The difficulty is that every participant remains sovereign. Gulf states themselves do not have identical interests. Their external partners face different constitutional requirements, domestic pressures and relationships with other powers. Some constraints are enduring; others reflect political choices that can change.

A government willing to provide intelligence may be unwilling to deploy forces. Another may support maritime protection but oppose an operation on land. Those limits should be understood before a crisis, when there is still time to plan around them.

Overlapping partnerships also carry risks. They can duplicate effort, create false expectations or draw countries into disputes they intended to avoid. Clear responsibilities and consultation procedures are essential. Adding agreements without clarifying what they deliver would produce more complexity without more security.

Nor should we promise that such an architecture will deliver a long peace. The rivalries and political grievances shaping this region will not disappear because its governments cooperate more closely.

A more attainable objective is relative peace and security: fewer opportunities for coercion, crises contained before they widen, and civilian life less exposed to each new confrontation. That means reducing the frequency and consequences of violence while continuing to work towards durable settlements. Permanent emergency cannot become an acceptable destination.

Gulf states should use this moment to connect their partnerships, strengthen their own capabilities and establish clearer limits on escalation. The aim is a region with more partners able to act together, and fewer crises capable of dragging everyone into war.

articles.title: An Ohio woman signed a deal to sell her 62-acre farm to a land conservancy for $350,000 and died the day after it took effect; an appeals court has ruled the money goes to the heirs in her will, not those on her deed
articles.summary: An Ohio woman who agreed to sell her 62-acre farm to a land conservancy for $350,000 died just one day after the sale agreement took effect, leaving a
articles.body: An Ohio woman who agreed to sell her 62-acre farm to a land conservancy for $350,000 died just one day after the sale agreement took effect, leaving a legal dispute over who should receive the money. In a ruling issued on 5 October 2026, Ohio’s Eleventh District Court of Appeals held that the proceeds belong to the heirs named in Eleanor M. Hovanick’s will, rather than the beneficiaries listed on her transfer-on-death deed, according to the court’s opinion.The decision resolves a question of first impression in Ohio appellate courts: Whether a valid transfer-on-death designation survives when the property owner signs a binding sale contract before dying. The court concluded that it does not, because the sale agreement converted Hovanick’s interest in the land into a right to receive money, which then passed through her estate. Read more details about this case, as per the court report, here:The farm and the deedHovanick owned nearly 62 acres of real estate in Orwell, Ohio. In November 2010, she recorded a transfer-on-death designation affidavit naming Ann M. Zimmer, Carol Mohr, Michael Hovanick and Peggy Rodriguez as beneficiaries who would receive the land when she died.A transfer-on-death deed allows an owner to name people who will receive real estate after death without going through probate. Under Ohio law, the designation does not affect the owner’s present ownership, and the named beneficiaries acquire no interest in the property until the owner dies.Hovanick never recorded a new affidavit revoking the 2010 designation. That fact became central to the dispute, because the beneficiaries argued that the deed should still control who received the value of the farm.The sale agreementOn 18 July 2021, Hovanick signed a will leaving all of her property in equal shares to Michael Hovanick and Lucinda Hovanick. The will specifically left nothing to Carol Mohr, while Zimmer and Rodriguez had already died before Hovanick.Months later, on 19 December 2021, Hovanick signed a purchase and sale agreement to sell the Orwell farm to the Western Reserve Land Conservancy for $350,000. She also signed a charitable pledge agreement to donate $50,000 of the gross sale proceeds to the conservancy to help offset its acquisition costs.The conservancy signed the agreement on 27 December 2021, making it effective that day. Hovanick died the following day, 28 December 2021, while still listed as the owner of record of the property.What the heirs arguedLucinda Hovanick, who served as executor of the estate, argued that the sale proceeds should be distributed under Eleanor’s will. Her position was that the binding sale agreement had changed the nature of Eleanor’s interest from real estate into a right to receive payment.Carol Mohr and Michele Boiarski, the granddaughter of the deceased, disagreed. They argued that the 2010 transfer-on-death affidavit remained valid because Eleanor had never formally revoked it, meaning the land and its sale proceeds should pass to the named beneficiaries rather than through the will.The dispute did not concern whether the conservancy could buy the farm. Both sides accepted that the sale could proceed; the question was whether the $350,000 belonged to the estate or to the people named on the transfer-on-death deed.The court’s reasoningThe appeals court affirmed the probate court’s decision and held that the doctrine of equitable conversion applied. In simple terms, once a binding contract to sell land exists, equity treats the seller’s interest as a right to the purchase money rather than ownership of the land itself.Because Hovanick and the conservancy had entered into a written, unconditional and enforceable sale agreement before her death, the court found that her interest in the farm had been converted into personal property. That right to payment became part of her estate and was therefore governed by her will.The court stressed that a transfer-on-death affidavit concerns only real property. Once the land was validly sold under a pre-death contract, the remaining interest was money, and the statute does not provide for a transfer-on-death beneficiary to receive money.Why the will controlledThe court also looked closely at Hovanick’s actions in the months before her death. Five months before signing the sale agreement, she had made a will that divided her property between Michael and Lucinda Hovanick and explicitly excluded Carol Mohr.The court said those actions showed a clear intention for the value of the farm to pass through her estate under the will. It concluded that treating her failure to record a revocation as more important than her deliberate decision to sell the property would elevate inaction over her expressed wishes.The ruling does not say that Hovanick’s contract revoked the transfer-on-death affidavit. Instead, the affidavit remained technically valid but had no real property left to transfer, because the sale agreement had already converted the owner’s interest into a claim for sale proceeds.What it means for OhioThe decision is significant because it is the first Ohio appellate ruling to address this exact interaction between a transfer-on-death deed and a pre-death sale contract. It confirms that an owner can still sell property after recording such a deed, and that the buyer’s right to purchase the land is protected.For families, the case highlights the importance of keeping estate-planning documents aligned with real-life decisions. A transfer-on-death deed may name one set of beneficiaries, but a later will and a signed sale agreement can determine what happens to the value of the property.The court’s ruling means the $350,000 from the conservancy will be treated as an asset of Hovanick’s estate. Subject to the agreed $50,000 charitable pledge, the remaining proceeds are to be distributed under her will, to Michael and Lucinda Hovanick rather than to the beneficiaries named on the 2010 deed.You use AI every day. articles.title: Couple accused of killing registered sex offender in pre-planned stabbing in Arizona desert
articles.summary: A couple allegedly planned the stabbing of a registered sex offender in a desert area in Arizona and now face first-degree homicide charges, police say.
articles.body: An Arizona couple was arrested after allegedly stabbing a registered sex offender to death in a desert area of the state, according to authorities. Jacob Middlebrook, 35, and his girlfriend, Layne McIntosh, 36, were initially taken into custody for second-degree homicide in the death of 29-year-old Arron Christopher Warren, Bullhead City Police said on social media. Police began investigating after a motorist found a dead man on the side of the road in the 3100 block of Silver Creek Road on Saturday. The circumstances surrounding the man’s death appeared suspicious, so detectives were called to the scene to conduct a homicide investigation. MICHIGAN DECISION FORCES REMOVAL OF DISGRACED SPORTS DOCTOR LARRY NASSAR FROM SEX OFFENDER REGISTRY Detectives later identified the man as Warren, a Bullhead City "transient." Detectives also identified a possible suspect and discovered that the victim’s vehicle was missing. Hours later, Las Vegas Metro Police assisted Bullhead City investigators and located the victim’s vehicle parked at a casino in Laughlin, Nevada. Middlebrook and McIntosh were taken into custody by Las Vegas Metro Police and booked into the Clark County Detention Center in Las Vegas, where they will be held until they can be extradited to Mohave County, Arizona. On Monday, the pair's charges were upgraded to first-degree homicide. CALIFORNIA SHERIFF FIGHTS PLAN TO HOUSE CONVICTED SEX PREDATOR NEAR GIRL SCOUT CAMP Investigators determined that the two were also "local transients" who had known the victim for the past few months. "Detectives discovered that the couple had expressed distaste for registered sex offenders and had planned the homicide in advance," Bullhead City police said. "The couple reportedly pre-determined the desert location where they intended to leave Warren’s body. They also reportedly measured furniture/beds that could be large enough to cover the victim’s body along the side of the road. Warren was a registered Level 2 sex offender," the post added. Bullhead City Police Chief Paul George said the department updates the community when certain registered sex offenders move in or change addresses but that he "will not tolerate anyone using this information as a reason to threaten, intimidate, harass or harm another person." "When a Level 2 or Level 3 sex offender moves into our area or, more commonly, changes addresses, the Bullhead City Police Department shares that information as a public service to help keep residents informed," he said in a statement. "While required notifications are mailed to residents living within an approximate 1,000 feet radius of an offender’s registered address, we go a step further by sharing these notifications on social media to reach a broader audience. Our goal is to provide information, not create fear or alarm. We believe an informed community is a safer community." Our responsibility is to protect our community, keep residents informed and to enforce the law. We take all three of these seriously," George continued.

articles.title: Download 2027 line-up: Blink-182 to headline on festival debut
articles.summary: Evanescence and Bring Me The Horizon will also top the bill at the rock and metal festival.
articles.body:
Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.

The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.

Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.

US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.

The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.

It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.

The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.

The choice of Emily upset some fans , who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.

Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.

They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.

Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.

British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.

The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.

That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.

Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.

But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".

Download bills itself as a festival "spanning the full spectrum of rock, metal, punk, emo, hardcore, alternative and classic rock".

It called this year's line-up "bigger, better and bolder than ever" and said it features "something for everyone, from huge artists to electric newcomers".

Other acts announced include Turnstile, Faith No More, Body Count ft. Ice-T and Malevolence - with the festival saying more will be revealed.

Some pre-sales are currently available but tickets go on general sale at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.

In recent years Download has also featured pop acts and surprise guests, with the Vengaboys an unlikely addition to 2024's line-up.

And Dogstar - the band formed by actor Keanu Reeves - performed in 2026.

articles.title: Three times faster, harder to intercept: Indian Army sets sights on 540 jet-powered kamikaze drones
articles.summary: The drones of the next war may not buzz like the slow propeller-driven Shaheds of recent years. They may arrive at nearly three times the speed.
articles.body: The drones of the next war may not buzz like the slow propeller-driven Shaheds of recent years. They may arrive at nearly three times the speed. The Indian Army will begin field trials of indigenous jet-powered kamikaze drones this week at Pokhran in Rajasthan, in a programme estimated at Rs 2,000 crore. Under the Jet Based Kamikaze Drone System (JBKDS), the Army plans to buy 540 units through the Fast Track Procurement scheme. It is the first time the Army is acquiring high-speed kamikaze attack drones under a dedicated programme.The competition is limited to Indian companies. Around 60 responded to the Army's Request for Information (RFI) in July 2026, 18 submitted bids and 11 qualified for the trials. Those named include Bharat Forge with VEDA Aeronautics, NIBE, Adani Defence, SMPP with NewSpace Research and Technologies, Tonbo, Munitions India Limited and Apollo Micro Systems. Vendors must show not just the drone but a complete operational package, including vehicles to carry it and mission planning and briefing vehicles.Why jetsKamikaze drones, or loitering munitions, hover over an area, find a target and crash into it with an explosive payload. Propeller-driven types fly at 150 to 200 kmph, while jet-powered ones reach around 450 kmph, which gets them to their targets sooner and makes them harder to intercept. The Air Force used Harpy and Harop drones against Pakistani radars and command posts during the 88-hour Operation Sindoor, and the war in Ukraine has shown how cheap platforms can hit military infrastructure.Iran fielded the jet-powered Shahed-238 in 2023, and Russia went on to the Geran-3, 4 and 5. The Geran-4 flies at up to eight km at 450 to 500 kmph with a range of over 700 km, and Ukrainian intelligence estimates Russia makes around 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month. Ukraine has used F-16s and interceptor drones against them.India's building blocksIndia is working on the key part, the engine. The Defence Research and Development Organisation's Gas Turbine Research Establishment (GTRE) has developed a 350 kg class expendable turbojet, the kind used in cruise missiles and jet-powered loitering munitions. It sits just below the 450 kg class Small Turbofan Engine for the Long-Range Land Attack Cruise Missile. GTRE works with Azad Engineering, and firms such as DG Propulsion, Nabhdrishti Aerospace and Paninian Aerospace are also entering the field.The Army has also taken delivery of 106 jet-powered Agniveg drones from SMPP, 100 operational and six for training. Agniveg flies at up to 450 kmph, is claimed to hit within five metres of its target and is built to resist jamming and spoofing. If the trials go well, the Army will have a domestic answer to a kind of strike weapon that is changing how wars are fought.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Huang, Lutnick summoned to testify to US Senate
articles.summary: The Banking Committee says the ex-tech CEO and the commerce secretary could face legal action if they fail to appear.
articles.body:
United States lawmakers have summoned Nvidia’s former CEO Jensen Huang and US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify about their roles in the scandal rocking the tech company.

Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott on Thursday requested that they appear in a public hearing on December 3. He threatened that the pair would face subpoenas should they refuse.

Huang resigned earlier on Thursday amid revelations of extramarital affairs, including with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China.

The firm, which manufactures advanced chips powering artificial intelligence, has since seen its market value fall below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025.

Amid the scandal, President Donald Trump’s administration faces allegations that Nvidia did not receive proper scrutiny for its exports of advanced semiconductors to China.

Lawmakers have also accused Lutnick’s Commerce Department of refusing to add dozens of Chinese companies to a US trade blacklist.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology,” Scott wrote in a post on X. “The American people deserve answers.”

Three other House committees have asked Huang and Nvidia General Counsel Tim Teter to appear for separate hearings on December 1 and 2, or face subpoenas.

Under Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler was summoned for a December 3 hearing.

In a joint letter, the head of the Foreign Affairs Committee, Brian Mast, China Select Committee Chair John Moolenaar, and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford wrote that “there are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately.”

China has denied allegations of spying on the US. President Trump earlier defended Huang, calling him “honourable”.

Senator Richard Blumenthal voiced concern to Al Jazeera over allegations that Nvidia had donated $25,000 to the Trump administration.

China on Friday warned that the tightening of US regulations on the export of semiconductors would threaten the stability of global industry and supply chains.

Bejing “has consistently opposed the abuse of export control measures,” a foreign ministry spokeswoman said.

Amid the Nvidia scandal, US lawmakers have called for limits on exports of chip equipment to China.

articles.title: Who gets to tell the world’s news?
articles.summary: A look back at the Global South’s early efforts to challenge Western dominance of international news.
articles.body:
Daya Thussu was still a student when he landed a subediting desk job at the Press Trust of India (PTI), then India’s largest news agency.

It was the early 1980s, and the newsroom in New Delhi was alive with the clatter of telex machines delivering dispatches from across the world.

At his desk, Thussu, then in his mid-20s, worked through two very different streams of international news. One came from established Western agencies, including Reuters. The other arrived through a little-known network connecting newsrooms across Asia, Africa and Latin America.

“We would check the ticker to see what the story was and where it had come from,” Thussu says of his work with the Non-Aligned News Agencies Pool (NANAP). “It could be from anywhere - the Philippines, Iraq or across Africa. My job was to select stories that we would then send out to the PTI wires.”

The two streams of news offered different windows on the world. One came from established international agencies, largely based in Western capitals. The other represented an attempt by countries long dependent on those agencies to tell their own stories.

Describing it as a cumbersome process in which copy was edited by hand and then given to a typist to put into the system, Thussu nevertheless remembers it as valuable training. “It was great hands-on training for someone like me who was very interested in international news and was pursuing a PhD in international relations at Jawaharlal Nehru University,” he says from his home in London.

For decades, a handful of Western news agencies had dominated the flow of international reporting. Now, countries that had fought for political independence were trying something else: exchanging news directly with one another without relying on London, Paris or Washington, DC, to tell their stories.

It was an experiment born of the Non-Aligned Movement, a coalition of countries seeking a path independent of the rival superpowers of the Cold War.

And it raised a question that remains pertinent today: Who decides what the rest of the world gets to know?
