articles.title: Scorpio vs Aquarius: Why These Two Zodiac Signs May Be Harder to Influence Than You Think
articles.summary: Picture two people in the same office. One rarely speaks in meetings, but somehow every major decision passes through them first.
articles.body: Picture two people in the same office. One rarely speaks in meetings, but somehow every major decision passes through them first. The other speaks constantly, pitches new ideas, builds a team around a cause and rallies the whole floor behind a change. Both have power. They just use it in completely different ways. Astrology often maps these two styles onto Scorpio and Aquarius, two signs that sit at a tense angle in the zodiac and see influence through opposite lenses.Two Fixed Signs at Right AnglesScorpio and Aquarius are both fixed signs. Fixed signs hold steady. They’re loyal to their views and slow to change course. That shared stubbornness is one reason these two signs can clash so hard.They also sit 90 degrees apart, forming a square. In astrology, squares create friction. The signs involved want different things and pull against each other.Their elements explain the difference. Scorpio is water, ruled by feelings and inner experience. Aquarius is air, ruled by thought and social connection. One goes deep. The other goes wide.Their rulers add contrast. Scorpio is traditionally ruled by Mars and, in modern astrology, by Pluto. Aquarius is traditionally ruled by Saturn and, in modern astrology, by Uranus. Pluto is about hidden control and big change. Uranus is about sudden breakthroughs and breaking rules.Scorpio: Power Through DepthScorpio’s power is personal and quiet. It works through understanding people better than they understand themselves.A Scorpio notices motives, weak spots and unspoken loyalties. In a family business, the Scorpio sibling may never hold the top title. But they know where the money goes, who owes whom and which relative will side with which. That knowledge is power.Scorpio also holds power through emotional intensity. People feel the weight of a Scorpio’s attention. Their approval matters. Their silence can feel heavy.This kind of power works best one-on-one or in small circles. Scorpios prefer influence they can control directly, often through trust built over years.The shadow side is control. Scorpios can hold on to power through secrecy or by keeping others slightly dependent. Learning to share influence and trust others with information is a major lesson for the sign.Aquarius: Power Through Ideas and GroupsAquarius takes the opposite route. Its power is public and collective. Aquarians influence people through ideas, causes and networks.An Aquarius might start a residents’ association, build an online community or push their company to adopt new technology. They rarely seek personal control. They want systems to change for everyone.Aquarians are often comfortable being unpopular for a while if they believe they’re right. Their strength lies in seeing where society is heading before others do.But Aquarian power has its own shadow. It can become detached. An Aquarius may care deeply about humanity in general and still miss one friend's hurt feelings. They can also become rigid about their principles, convinced that everyone else just hasn’t caught up yet.When the Two MeetIn relationships, Scorpio and Aquarius often find each other fascinating at first. Scorpio is drawn to Aquarius’s originality. Aquarius respects Scorpio’s depth. Then the friction starts. Scorpio wants emotional closeness and exclusivity. Aquarius wants space and freedom. Both refuse to back down easily.When these partnerships work, it’s usually because each learns from the other. Scorpio learns to loosen its grip. Aquarius learns that feelings aren’t a problem to solve.The current sky puts these two signs in direct conversation. Pluto, Scorpio’s modern ruler, is moving through Aquarius for many years. Many astrologers link this transit with power shifting toward technology, networks and collective movements. And with Scorpio season starting on October 23, the Sun in Scorpio will form a square with Pluto in Aquarius in late October. That contact often brings power struggles to the surface, whether at home, at work, or in public life.Get the latest astrology news and horoscope updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Second car bomb hits Russia in two days
articles.summary: A onetime spokesman for a pro-Russian former prime minister of Ukraine was wounded by a car bomb in Moscow on Friday, Russian media reported.
articles.body: A onetime spokesman for a pro-Russian former prime minister of Ukraine was wounded by a car bomb in Moscow on Friday, Russian media reported. The Kommersant newspaper reported that Sergei Zavorotniy, once a top aide of Mykola Azarov, who served as Ukraine’s prime minister from 2010 to 2014, was hospitalized after a car exploded on a street in Chertanovo, a district of the Russian capital. It was the second car bombing in Russia in successive days. Moscow has blamed Ukraine for previous assassinations of senior military officials and people linked to Russia’s war effort. There was no immediate comment from Ukraine on Friday. Ren TV and the 112 Telegram channel both reported that Zavorotniy had lost his left arm in the attack, and that he was in hospital with a concussion, rib fractures and other injuries. The Baza Telegram channel published a photograph of a black four-door car with a smashed windshield, doors and front bumper on a city street. Russia’s Investigative Committee, which handles serious crimes, said it had opened an investigation into the incident. Zavorotniy’s former boss Azarov fled to Russia in 2014, when Ukraine’s Maidan Revolution ousted pro-Russian president Viktor Yanukovych after he broke a promise to develop closer ties with the European Union. Azarov told Russia’s TASS state news agency on Friday that he had no information about the car bomb, except that Zavorotniy had survived. The explosion was the latest in a series of apparent assassination attempts inside Russia. On Thursday a member of the Russian military was killed in a car bomb in St Petersburg. Ukrainian sources have claimed responsibility in some cases, while denying others. Kyiv has not commented on Thursday’s attack.

articles.title: GPs, police and pharmacies among UK services affected by Microsoft outage
articles.summary: Major airports and intelligence services are unaffected while the government is assessing the impact on its services.
articles.body:
GPs, police and pharmacies are among UK services affected by a global outage on some Microsoft platforms.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report. MPs are also affected.

Microsoft has said the problem was caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers and that the fixes it had put in place were "not taking as expected".

Major airports and UK intelligence services have been unaffected by the outage, while a minister said officials were assessing the extent of the impact on government services.

Tim Frank, a GP in Penzance, told the BBC that they had received no emails today, and that if the problem with Microsoft's messaging platform Teams persisted, this could cause delays and affect patient care.

Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

Microsoft scrambles to solve global outage affecting Outlook and Teams but says fixes not going 'as expected'

What we know about the global Microsoft outage

A spokesperson for the National Pharmacy Association said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".

Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and North Yorkshire Police have all issued statements saying online forms may be affected by the outage. They have urged people to call 101 with time-critical but non-emergency reports.

South Wales Police and Dyfed-Powys Police have also reported similar issues and are asking people to call if they need to get in touch.

The London Ambulance Service's critical platforms do not use Microsoft so are unaffected by the outage.

Similarly, operations at Heathrow, Manchester and Stansted airports are operating as usual.

Defence minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that the government was "assessing the impact" of the outage on its systems and would issue a statement once this was completed.

A government spokesperson said it was "working closely" with Microsoft to assess "any impact on government services" by the company's outage.

It is understood that UK intelligence operations have been unaffected. While some elements of the security services use Microsoft tools, they have a separate system for secret operations.

MPs are unable to access their parliamentary accounts, however. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place to allow the day's business to go ahead.

Some teachers have reported being unable to access their calendars, emails and files on cloud servers.

Throttled traffic 'just like on a motorway'

Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage, which has affected Outlook, Teams and Copilot.

The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly available", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain.

"Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained.

"Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here."

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others".

"Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge."

His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption.

Moore added that "good old-fashioned phone lines" seemed to be "the strongest form of communication, especially today".

Some people were initially glad to hear about the outage - especially as it has occurred just before the weekend.

Martin told the BBC that waking up to no new emails was "absolute bliss" until he realised "today is a crucial day to conclude a business deal".
